paras: The attempted lynching of Charles Cook took place at Columbus, Indiana, on the night of September 20, 1882, when a band of masked men went after Cook, whom the dispatch called "a notorious wife beater," with the object of lynching him. Cook escaped, and the episode reached the press only as a one-sentence telegraphic item; none of the reports gives his race.

According to a Columbus dispatch dated September 21, "a mob of fifty masked men" called on Cook the previous night intending to lynch him. A German-language version printed in Baltimore put the band at 30 and said it forced its way into Cook's house during the night. Cook, that account added, had got wind of the plan in time and fled, and the Maysville Evening Bulletin said simply that "He had skipped."
No report of arrests, charges against the masked men, or any later proceedings against Cook appears in the coverage.

The Wheeling Register ran the dispatch on September 22 under the headline "After a Wife Measuer" [Beater], repeating the dispatch's label for Cook without comment. On September 23 the Maysville Evening Bulletin placed it among its "News Brevities," and Der Deutsche Correspondent of Baltimore carried a translated version among other brief news items. All three treated the attempt as a curiosity of the wire, accepting the wife-beating charge as the reason for the band's visit and raising no question about the masked men.
The reports differ on the size of the band, fifty in the Wheeling Register and 30 in Der Deutsche Correspondent, and only the German version says the men entered the house.
